title: Earth Screening Generates Distinct Signal Sidebands in Ultralight Dark
excerpt: Researchers calculate how Earth screening creates distinctive frequency sidebands in background-induced forces from quadratically coupled ultralight scalar dark matter.
content:
Theoretical physicists have developed a complete calculation of the background-induced, composition-dependent forces generated by quadratically coupled ultralight scalar dark matter beyond the spherically symmetric approximation. In a study published in the Journal of High Energy Physics, researchers Thomas Bouley, Xucheng Gan, Hailin Xu, and Tien-Tien Yu examine the physical behavior of this candidate substance. The authors establish that quadratically coupled ultralight scalar dark matter behaves as a coherent classical field whose direct interactions with standard matter can induce a composition-dependent force mediated entirely through the ambient dark matter background.

To model the detailed interaction beyond spherical symmetry, the research team implemented a partial-wave treatment of dark-matter scattering. By using this mathematical treatment, the authors determined the angular dependence of the background-induced force. In doing so, they derived an analytic description that remains fully valid even when the characteristic wavelength of the ultralight dark matter is substantially smaller than the physical radius of the Earth.

The analysis reveals for the first time that screening by the Earth generates a characteristic frequency-band structure. According to the investigation, this Earth screening splits the anticipated signal into multiple distinct sidebands, creating a distinctive experimental signature for detection efforts. The team further established that the relative amplitudes of these sidebands vary on an annual cycle as a satellite’s Sun-synchronous orbital plane precesses in step with the Earth’s orbital revolution around the Sun. This cyclic behavior enabled the researchers to construct a complete signal template for observational searches.

As a direct application of their theoretical findings, the authors re-evaluated experimental constraints from the MICROSCOPE satellite mission. The MICROSCOPE experiment currently provides the strongest laboratory limits on equivalence-principle violations caused by ultralight dark matter. Furthermore, the researchers showed that proposed future space-based equivalence-principle experiments, specifically Galileo Galilei and STE-QUEST, can significantly enhance their detection sensitivity to ultralight scalar dark matter by incorporating this comprehensive frequency-band information into their data analyses.
